title: Contempt for instructional time
author: Rod J. Naquin
summary: High school teacher Rod Naquin opens with the knock on his locked classroom door that interrupts a discussion at its best moment and uses it to argue that schools habitually treat class time as the default place for everything else. He draws on Matthew Kraft and Manuel Monti-Nussbaum's Providence study, which counted about 15 external interruptions a day and estimated 10 to 20 lost instructional days a year, and on Lawrence Leonard's Louisiana work showing that administrators badly undercount interruptions. The larger cost is momentum, since a thirty-second announcement takes minutes to recover from, especially in discussion based lessons. He points to schools that have done better, including a principal who removed hallway duties and Noble Schools building pull-out services into the timetable. His practical contribution is a talk move called Name the Minute, which asks which minute of instruction a proposal takes and whether it could happen elsewhere, ideally backed by a one-week tally of interruptions.
points: Small interruptions add up to roughly 2,000 a year per classroom and an estimated 10 to 20 lost days of instruction.
The people who allocate time are the furthest from its cost, as administrators in both Providence and Louisiana guessed far fewer interruptions than teachers and observers recorded.
Rules fade without monitoring, so Kraft recommends teachers track interruptions and the school decide together which are necessary.
Giving pull-out services and hallway coverage their own scheduled place protects teaching time better than adding minutes without intention.
Name the Minute offers a non-confrontational question leaders and counselors can ask before touching class time, and a one-week tally makes the cost hard to dismiss.
quotes: So by “contempt,” I don’t mean anyone looks down on teaching. I mean a structural habit of treating class time as the default place to put everything else.
In their observations, classrooms were interrupted about 15 times a day. That’s more than 2,000 interruptions a year.
The researchers estimate this costs about three and a half minutes of instruction every hour. Over a year, that comes to 10 to 20 lost days.
The intercom announcement is maybe 30 seconds long, but it takes a few minutes for the teacher to sort of be able to get the class back on track.
In Providence, researchers counted about 15 interruptions a day. Administrators guessed 58 percent fewer, which is less than half the real number.
Rules alone won’t last, though. Kraft recommends a shared process: teachers track interruptions, and the school decides together which ones are necessary.

Here’s the talk move: Name the Minute. When someone proposes something that touches class time, such as a pull-out, an announcement, or a “quick” visit, ask: “Which minute of instruction is this taking, and is that trade worth it to the student who loses it?
